explanation: Habitual action with singular subject 'He' takes present simple 'washes'.
'Next month' signals a planned future action: 'will go'.
An ongoing past action interrupted by another takes past continuous: 'was waiting'.
The bathing was already in progress when they arrived: past continuous 'was bathing'.
'One of the eggs' is a singular subject, taking 'was'.
'Sought after' is the standard passive idiom for being in demand.
'Since last week' with an unfinished state takes present perfect: 'has been'.
'For months' with a state continuing to now takes present perfect negative: 'haven't heard'.
An action continuing up to a past point of reference takes past perfect continuous: 'had been sitting'.
First conditional 'if' clauses use present simple even for future meaning: 'works'.
A main clause plus a subordinate 'because' clause makes this a complex sentence.
Two independent clauses joined by a semicolon form a compound sentence.
A single independent clause with no subordinate clause is a simple sentence.
The subordinate clause 'wherever you go' makes this a complex sentence.
Two independent clauses joined by 'but' form a compound sentence.
The subordinate clause 'when I was younger' makes this a complex sentence.
Two independent clauses joined by 'and' form a compound sentence.
The subordinate clause 'because he did not know the route well' makes this a complex sentence.
One subject with a compound verb ('jumped and landed') and no second independent clause is a simple sentence.
It has a subordinate 'because' clause plus two independent clauses joined by 'so' -- compound-complex.
Keeping the present-perfect tense of the original in active voice gives 'He has brought us the news.'
The past-tense active 'created' becomes past-tense passive: 'was created'.
'Although he was X' standardly reduces to 'In spite of being X' as a simple sentence.
'How kind of you to visit us!' is the standard exclamatory transformation.
The optative 'O that...' becomes the assertive statement 'I wish that I could fly like birds.'
'If...will' conditionals convert to compound sentences with 'and': 'Speak the truth and you will be honoured.'
'To earn money' expands into the complex-sentence purpose clause 'that he might earn money.'
'Better than any other student' converts to the superlative 'the best student.'
'So...that...cannot' reduces to the simple-sentence pattern 'too...to': 'too weak to move about.'
'No other boy...as tall as' converts to the comparative 'taller than any other boy.'
The three events combine using a participial opener: 'The dinner getting over, the guests were shown out and they got into their cars.'
'It is very hot. One cannot go out' combines idiomatically as 'It is too hot to go out.'
The first action becomes a participle describing the second: 'Standing on tip-toe she reached for the mangoes on the tree.'
The two facts combine as 'I still have few chapters in the novel to finish.'
'All agreed' becomes the adverb 'unanimously': 'They unanimously decided to start a travel group.'
Two abilities of the same subject combine naturally with 'both...and': 'Ani speaks both English and French.'
An imperative plus a warning combines with 'otherwise': 'Get inside, otherwise you may catch cold.'
The three facts combine into a single noun-clause sentence: 'His statement that she was honest was right.'
'Not only...but also' links the two qualities of Mohan naturally.
'James' friendship is reduced to an appositive: 'James, my friend, is the son of a doctor.'
'Exotic' means strikingly unusual or foreign, closest to 'Unusual'.
'Rectify' means to put right or correct, closest to 'Mend'.
'Bluster' involves loud, aggressive talk often carrying an implied threat.
'Reticence' means reserve or reluctance to speak freely.
'Brash' describes bold, aggressive self-confidence.
A 'renegade' is one who deserts a cause or group -- a rebel.
'Retribution' means punishment inflicted in return for a wrong.
'Haggle' means to bargain persistently over a price.
A 'connoisseur' is an expert judge in matters of taste, especially the arts.
'Zenith' means the highest point, matching 'Pinnacle'.
'Panacea' is the standard word for a cure-all remedy.
A 'gourmet' is one with refined, discerning taste in food.
'Sporadic' describes something occurring at irregular intervals.
A 'souvenir' is an object kept as a reminder of an event or place.
'Nepotism' names the practice of favouring one's own family members.
'Judicious' means done with sound judgment.
A 'boulevard' is precisely defined as a broad, tree-lined road.
A 'rhinologist' specializes in diseases of the nose (from Greek 'rhino-').
'Opaque' means not able to be seen through.
An 'octagon' is a geometric figure with eight sides.
'A better job' is the natural collocation for earning more money.
Ambitious managers are 'success oriented'.
'Haven't had any news' is the standard negative-context quantifier.
'Interrupt' fits breaking into someone's speech.
'Inoffensive' fits a mild, unthreatening manner, matching 'well-behaved'.
A tourist bureau sends 'information' about hotels.
A cut becoming 'infected' is the natural medical consequence described.
'Innovative' is the correctly spelled word; option (c) is a misspelling.
'Disturbed' best contrasts with the manager's usual calm demeanor.
'Unless' expresses the necessary condition (a suit and tie) for entry.
German meteorologist H. Seilkopf is credited with coining the term 'jet stream' in 1939.
Section 66F of the IT Act, 2000 prescribes imprisonment for life as the maximum punishment for cyber terrorism.
'Returning to baseline' means returning to the normal, resting level.
'A man of your expense' misuses the word; it should refer to a man of your 'means' or 'position', not 'expense'.
A 'benign smile' (kind, gentle) is incongruous on the face of an 'angry man'.
It is self-contradictory to call an army 'invincible' and then say it 'surrendered'.
'Courting his feelings into words' misuses the word; the correct verb for expressing feelings in words is 'couching', not 'courting'.
Attributing 'peep' to trees personified stretches the word's normal usage of a quick, often secretive human glance; low confidence as the other three are standard idioms.
'Differ in protocol with one's standpoint' is a nonsensical use of 'protocol', which properly means an official procedure or plan.
An ongoing action at that past moment takes past continuous: 'was working'.
The guests leaving happened before the washing began: past perfect 'had left'.
A permanent, general fact takes present simple: 'stands'.
A completed action by a future point takes future perfect: 'will have qualified'.
Reported past hope with 'would' pairs with simple past 'hoped'.
'At present' with a temporary situation takes present continuous: 'is living'.
An action ongoing up to a future point takes future continuous: 'will be tending'.
'Know' is a stative verb and does not take continuous forms; past perfect 'had known' fits 'since long'.
'Consequent upon' is the standard idiomatic phrase meaning 'as a result of'.
'Regretfully' is the adverb expressing his regret while admitting the error.
'To provide for' is the infinitive form combining the two facts.
'Feeling tired' is the participial phrase replacing the first clause.
'If you are honest' is the adverb clause of condition expressing the same idea.
'To hear' is the infinitive expressing the cause of his gladness.
'So...that...cannot' reduces to the simple-sentence pattern 'too...to': 'too tired to stand'.
'With all his contacts...never' converts to a compound sentence joined by 'but'.
The superlative 'most useful of all' converts to the comparative pattern 'no other...as...as'.
The rhetorical question 'What though...?' asserts that it does not matter.
'You called me and here I am' reduces to the complex sentence 'As you called me, I am here.'
'With great promptitude' modifies the verb 'acted', making it an Adverb Phrase.
One subject with a compound verb ('served...and was released') and no second independent clause is a Simple Sentence.
'Of the soft blue sky' modifies the noun 'witchery', functioning as an Adjective Phrase.
'(that) you propose' is a relative clause modifying 'the plan' -- an Adjective Clause.
'The magistrate of this place' is an appositive phrase, not a clause, so the sentence remains Simple.
'That hath his quarrel just' is a relative clause modifying 'he' -- an Adjective Clause.
'That he was guilty' is the object of 'confessed' -- a Noun Clause.
The exclamation 'Alas!' carries into reported speech as 'exclaimed with sorrow'.
A reported yes/no question uses 'if/whether' and backshifts 'shall' to 'would': 'wondered if he would ever forget her'.
Taking the reporting verb as present-tense 'says' keeps 'will' unchanged, giving internally consistent tense; the source sentence's punctuation is ambiguous, so confidence is low.
Indirect past perfect 'had eaten' reverses to direct simple past: 'She ate the meal.'
A present-tense reporting verb 'says' requires no backshift, keeping 'is a good player'.
'Goodbye' derives from 'God be with you', traditionally classed as an Optative (wish) expression.
'None but truth triumphs' is a positive assertion phrased negatively, classed as an Affirmative sentence.
With no Optative option listed, 'I wish...' is classed under the broader declarative Assertive category.
'Better trained than yours' directly compares two things -- a Comparative sentence.
'Please help me' is a request/command -- an Imperative sentence.
'Guilty of playing fast and loose' is the standard idiom for being unreliable or careless with others' feelings.
'Guilty of a flagrant breach of promise' fits both blanks meaningfully.
Changes that are 'obvious' would not require any 'modifications'.
One cannot 'pardon' an 'egregious' (flagrantly bad) act of violence.
Having 'aptitude' for learning but no 'interest' in speaking fits the contrast.
'Each' is a singular determiner and takes the singular verb 'is'.
'No...and no...' subjects conventionally take the singular verb agreeing with the nearer noun: 'was'.
'Either' is singular and takes 'has'.
'The accountant and the cashier' are two distinct people, taking the plural verb 'have'.
'More than one man' is idiomatically treated as singular: 'was'.
'You see' has 'that boy' as its object, requiring the objective relative pronoun 'whom' in formal usage.
'Few men' (without 'a') means almost none, fitting 'free from faults'.
After 'It was', the subject of the relative clause 'that gave' takes the subjective pronoun 'I'.
'What did they fight for' asks about the reason/cause of the fight.
'A little tact' (some, positive sense) would have saved the situation.
'Either of the sisters' in a negative sentence means disliking both.
'Every loan' fixes the singular/plural mismatch in 'Each of the loan'.
'Taken up at' is the correct idiom for an issue being discussed at a meeting.
A 'lone wolf' is commonly glossed as someone who prefers to be alone, closest to 'lonely person' among the given options.
